comments.text: Canva Brush is a new vision-language model for design, built by Canva Research. It sees your design, understands how it’s put together, and makes the changes you ask for, from a single line of copy to every slide in a deck.Problem: Generating a design is hard for AI, but editing one is harder. The model has to understand what you want to change, how the design is structured, and what has to stay exactly as it is. Otherwise a simple edit request can come back with a pile of changes you didn’t ask for.Solution: Brush works through an agentic loop. It writes and runs code to adjust design elements, then inspects the page to guide its next step. Everything it creates is fully editable like any other Canva design, so you can take over in the editor whenever you want.What makes it different: It’s built for design editing, not general chat. Brush started from a leading open-weights model, which Canva post-trained on real design and editing tasks, then added large-scale reinforcement learning with a reward system that scores visual quality, layout, and whether the task was completed as requested. Canva says its definition of “good” is set by professional designers on its team. Per Canva, it’s up to 69% faster and 46% lower cost per edit task than Canva’s previous design agent, and in internal testing it matched or exceeded the previous setup on most editing tasks.Key features:Restyle an image or design, like changing the colour scheme, the weather or the vibeChange a multi-page design in one prompt, instead of editing every header by handRemix a design for another channel, like turning a slide into an Instagram graphicFully editable output, with every element still yours to changeSelect “Brush” from the dropdown in Canva AIWho it’s for: Canva users who spend time on repetitive design edits, from solo creators to teams working on multi-page decks and campaigns.Try it by opening a design in the editor or going to Canva AI, and read the announcement. P.S. I hunt the latest and greatest launches in tech, SaaS and AI, follow to be notified → @rohanrecommends

today.name: fastbrowse
today.description: A fast open-source browser agent. It reads every button, link and field on the page and has a System One model (ex: jev) pick the next step from that list. If it's unsure, it falls back to a standard model model. Fast, cheap, and every answer provides a citation.
today.category: Open Source • Developer Tools • Artificial Intelligence

comments.text: Hey Product Hunt, I'm Furqan, one of the makers of fastbrowse.Browser agents have become exceptionally popular, but there's some huge problems. They're slow, expensive and miss easy tasks.A lot of them take a screenshot and have a slow model decide every step, so each task takes a while and the bill adds up.Fastbrowse reads the elements on the page instead. Every button, link and field is handed to a System One model (like Jev) with a list of choices. This model decies what to do next, when it isn't sure, fastbrowse falls back to a LLM to get it right. And because it only picks from what's on the page, it can't click something that isn't there.We tested this against the latest open-source browser agents agent: same sign-in and add-to-cart task on a demo shop, three runs each.fastbrowse took 25.7 seconds and $0.020 a run. Browser Use took 42.2 seconds and $0.045. Both got it right every time. On a wider 46-task benchmark against Browser Use's hosted agent running Claude Opus, our median task cost $0.026 vs $0.284. 99.2% of tasks passed. Fastbrowse produces citations for everything it referenced to get answers, so you can trust and verify the results.It's MIT licensed, and the code, the benchmark harness and the raw results are all on GitHub: https://github.com/agent-labs-dev/fastbrowse

Solid open source approach. Curious about the citation mechanism - how does it handle dynamic content and SPA updates? Also, what's the error recovery strategy when the model picks wrong paths? Comparing speed vs accuracy tradeoff vs proprietary agents would be interesting. Local deployment story is a big plus for privacy-focused teams.

Reading the elements instead of taking a screenshot for every step is the choice I'd want to understand first — especially with the 25.7-second, $0.020 run against Browser Use's 42.2 seconds and $0.045. When the small model is unsure and it falls back, does the citation trail still show which elements it was choosing between?

"Can't click something that isn't there" is an underrated feature. Half of browser-agent debugging is discovering the button the model invented. Reading the DOM first is the right kind of boring. Congrats on the launch!

Seeing the list of element choices alongside the fallback would be useful when debugging a run. It gives you a way to check what the agent actually had available at that step.

Congrats on the launch, Furqan! Sharing the benchmark harness and raw results on GitHub is the kind of transparency that makes me trust a tool right away.Question from the design side: since fastbrowse reads the elements instead of screenshots, how does it handle icon-only buttons with no label, or canvas-heavy UIs where there's barely any DOM to read? Feels like this approach quietly rewards apps with good accessibility, which I love.We're launching on Product Hunt today too, good luck! 🚀

comments.text: JST-2 is Viggle’s physics-native world foundation model. It generates 3D scenes, characters and full-body motion in one shared 3D world.Problem: Building 3D content is split into separate, slow jobs. Scenes, characters, rigging and animation each need their own tools and specialists, and rigging and skinning alone can take hours and decide how a character moves afterward.Solution: JST-2 handles all three in one model. Viggle’s JST architecture represents the world as persistent 3D “atoms” with learned attributes and dynamics, encodes them as Physics-Native Tokens, and decodes them into images or 3D Gaussian splats.What makes it different: Characters come with motion built in, so there’s no separate rigging or skinning step, and scenes can be explored without rerunning the model. Per Viggle, a 3D scene takes about one second to generate, against about 5 to 6 minutes for Marble, at an inference cost below $0.01 per scene. Full disclosure — I'm a big fan of Anthropic and actually built an app that works exclusively with Claude Desktop for secure local file search. So I've spent a lot of time thinking about this space.My concern with Cowork isn't the vision, it's the architecture. Agentic tasks burn through tokens fast (Anthropic says so themselves), so that $200/month cap can disappear quicker than you'd expect. And at that price, you'd want to use it for real work — but the whole thing requires giving Claude direct read/write/delete access to your files. If you're handling client data, patient records, or anything regulated, you're basically out.The bigger issue is prompt injection. Anthropic admits "the chances of an attack are still non-zero" — and back in October 2025, researchers showed exactly that: a prompt injection against Claude that pulled up to 30MB of user data per request through Anthropic's own API. When you're talking about an agent with file system access, email connectors, and a browser, that's not some theoretical edge case.There's a reason some of us build tools where Claude can search your files without actually touching them. The agentic future is definitely coming, but "AI that can access everything" and "AI that keeps you in control" are two very different products for two very different users.
